INTERVIEW STATEMENT - JIM DELANEY

I am uneasy about how quickly AI tools have entered the classroom without enough attention to what may be lost. My biggest concern is that students can receive a convincing answer before they have developed the background needed to judge whether that answer is good. In technical subjects, a small error can matter. A command may be unsafe, a configuration may be inappropriate, or an explanation may sound reasonable while missing the real cause of a problem.

That uncertainty creates extra work for instructors. Instead of correcting a student's own misunderstanding, we may be forced to untangle a polished response generated by a system whose reasoning the student cannot explain. I find that frustrating. It becomes harder to tell whether a student has mastered the material, and harder to provide useful feedback when the submitted work does not reflect the student's actual thought process.

I am also concerned about dependency. Learning technical skills requires patience. Students need to read documentation, make mistakes, troubleshoot, and sometimes sit with a problem for a while. If AI always supplies the next command or suggests the answer immediately, students may never build the persistence that real support and infrastructure jobs demand. When the automated suggestion fails, they still need enough knowledge to continue on their own.

There may eventually be a sensible role for these tools, and I understand why employers are interested in them. But I do not think enthusiasm should outrun caution. We need strong rules about acceptable use, deliberate assessments, and clear evidence that students can perform essential tasks independently. Until I see those safeguards working consistently, I will remain doubtful about expanding AI use in my courses. The possibility of weakened fundamentals, inaccurate answers, and academic shortcuts makes me more concerned than excited.
